opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think a few things converged at once. If you look back a few years, the protein design field was really fragmented. You had a separate tool for every task: one model for structure prediction, another for sequence design, another for docking, and then a bunch of bespoke pipelines stitched together for things like binder design or antibody work. Each of those had its own assumptions and its own failure modes, and getting them to talk to each other was honestly half the work.

What changed is that structure prediction models got good enough, and general enough, that they started to look like a foundation you could build everything else on. Once you have a model that understands how proteins, nucleic acids, small molecules, and so on actually come together in three dimensions, it starts to feel like you've captured a lot of the underlying physics and chemistry implicitly. At that point the question becomes: why train a narrow model for each problem when you could have one model that actually understands molecular interactions and adapt it to design?

The other piece is that we'd seen this movie before in language and vision. Specialized models were state of the art right up until general models trained at scale started beating them, often on the specialists' own benchmarks. We had a strong prior that biology would follow a similar trajectory, especially once data, compute, and architectures matured enough. And when we started Chai, we felt we were right at that inflection point.

And practically, the thing that really matters for drug discovery is hit rate in the lab. If you can design binders or antibodies that actually work at meaningful rates on the first try, without screening millions of variants, that changes the economics of the whole enterprise. We started seeing signs that general models could do that, both in our own experiments and across the field. So it felt less like a speculative bet and more like the right time to commit fully, build the general model, and test it seriously against wet-lab validation instead of just in silico metrics.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there were a few things converging at once. When Joshua and I were doing our PhDs, and honestly for most of the last decade, protein design and protein structure prediction were really treated as separate problems with separate tools. You'd have one model for folding, another for docking small molecules, another for antibody design, and each of those was its own community with its own benchmarks and its own tricks. And that made sense when the models were small and data was scarce, because you had to bake in a lot of domain knowledge to get anything to work.

What changed, and I think AlphaFold 2 was the real inflection point, was that we saw that if you take a big enough architecture and the right training setup, the model learns a lot of that physics and biochemistry on its own. It doesn't need you to hand-engineer the inductive biases to the same degree. And then AlphaFold 3 and the work on co-folding showed that the same model could handle proteins, nucleic acids, small molecules, ions, all in one framework. Once you see that, the natural question is, why stop at structure prediction? If one model can represent all these molecular interactions, it should be able to reason about them generatively too.

The other piece was the practical side. We'd spent years watching drug discovery teams stitch together ten different tools, and every handoff between tools loses information. A generative model proposes a binder, a separate folding model scores it, a separate model estimates affinity, and none of them agree with each other. We thought a general model that could do all of that in a shared representation would just be more useful, not just more elegant. If you can ask it for a de novo binder against an arbitrary target and have it reason about the whole complex at once, that's a fundamentally different workflow for a wet lab team.

And honestly, timing-wise, the compute and the engineering talent were finally there. A few years ago a small team couldn't train models at this scale. Now we could. So it felt less like a bet and more like, this is clearly where the field is going, and we wanted to be the ones to build it well and make it accessible rather than wait for it to happen somewhere else.

astra-6.text:
I think it was the convergence of a few things. Structure prediction had gotten good enough that we could start asking a different question: instead of just predicting what a protein looks like, can we design one that does something useful? And the progress in general models suggested that learning across related tasks could be more powerful than building a separate system for each one.

Biology is a natural fit for that approach, because proteins don’t operate in isolation. They interact with other proteins, small molecules, DNA, and RNA. If you want to design those interactions, you want a model that can learn that shared context. So the bet for us was that a more general understanding of molecular interactions could become a foundation for protein design, rather than having to start from scratch for every new target.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we were seeing a convergence of a few things. The structural data was getting richer, the modeling approaches were becoming much more capable, and there was a real need to move beyond tools that solve one narrow part of protein design. If you want to design a molecule that does something useful, you have to think about its interactions—with other proteins, with small molecules, and with the broader biological context.

So the question for us was: could we build a model that learns a more general picture of those interactions, and then use that as a foundation for design? It felt like the ingredients were there to make meaningful progress, even though there was still a lot to figure out.
